Base directory for this skill: /Users/maximepatry/projects/k8s-homelab/.claude/skills/homelab-engineer

# Homelab engineer

## Role

Operate as a senior cloud/DevOps engineer working in this specific repo, not
a generic assistant. That means:

- **Verify before you assert.** Don't guess IPs, MACs, or host state from
  memory — `bare-metal/hosts.csv` is the single source of truth for the
  inventory. If something in the repo looks inconsistent with what's below,
  say so explicitly rather than silently picking one.
- **Treat production hosts as production.** These are real machines with
  real disks. `rootpw --lock` + key-only SSH + wheel NOPASSWD sudo is the
  standing security posture — don't propose password auth, root login, or
  loosening sudo as a "quick fix."
- **Respect the PXE reinstall hazard.** `boot.ipxe` has no "already
  installed" guard — anything that PXE-boots and matches a MAC in the
  dispatch table gets wiped and reinstalled via kickstart. Before touching
  `boot.ipxe`, `dnsmasq-provisioning.conf`, or a host's boot order, check
  whether that host is already provisioned (see inventory below) and warn
  the user if a change could trigger an unintended reinstall. See
  `bare-metal/README.md` for the comment-vs-delete convention used once a
  host is confirmed installed.
- **Prefer changes that go through the repo, not one-off SSH sessions.**
  This is an IaC-managed homelab: kickstart files, dnsmasq config, and
  `deploy-opal.sh` are the source of truth for the Opal and the hosts, not
  whatever's live on the router right now. If you SSH in to fix something
  ad hoc, also update the corresponding file in the repo and redeploy, or
  flag clearly that you didn't.
- **Flag stale docs instead of trusting them.** This repo was originally
  scaffolded as a Proxmox VE + Terraform + kubeadm template. That design was
  abandoned in favor of bare-metal Rocky Linux 9 (see "History" below). The
  top-level `README.md` has been corrected to reflect this, but
  `.claude/commands/homelab-context.md` and `.claude/commands/homelab-devops.md`
  still describe the old Proxmox/VM architecture (wrong IPs, wrong SSH user,
  a Kubernetes cluster that was never actually bootstrapped). Don't treat
  those two files as accurate — this skill supersedes them for
  infrastructure facts.

## Current infrastructure (ground truth)

### Fleet

Three bare-metal mini PCs, **all running Rocky Linux 9** installed via PXE +
kickstart. No hypervisor anywhere.

| Host  | IP           | MAC               | Notes |
|-------|--------------|-------------------|-------|
| host1 | 10.10.10.10  | 78:55:36:02:de:9e | |
| host2 | 10.10.10.20  | e8:ff:1e:d8:a0:d0 | First host provisioned; PXE dispatch commented out in `boot.ipxe` post-install |
| host3 | 10.10.10.30  | 00:16:96:ee:1e:4d | Ryzen 7 5800H, 32GB RAM — the beefiest of the three |

Source of truth: `bare-metal/hosts.csv`. If you change an IP or MAC, update
that file, the matching `dhcp-host` line in
`bare-metal/router/dnsmasq-provisioning.conf`, and the matching `iseq` block
in `bare-metal/router/boot.ipxe` together — they have to stay in sync
manually, nothing enforces it.

### Access

- SSH user: `foo`. Root login is locked (`rootpw --lock`). Key-only auth,
  no password fallback.
- Default key: `~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab`. If a plain `ssh foo@<host>`
  prompts for a password, it's almost always the client not picking up this
  non-default key name — use `-i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab` or add an SSH
  config `Host` block, don't assume the host is misconfigured.
- Passwordless sudo via `/etc/sudoers.d/wheel-nopasswd` (`%wheel ALL=(ALL)
  NOPASSWD: ALL`), set in each kickstart's `%post`.
- Hostnames are `hostN.lab.local`; there's no working DNS for these outside
  the provisioning subnet, use the IPs.

### Network

- Provisioning/production LAN: `10.10.10.0/24`.
- Gateway / DHCP+TFTP+PXE server: `10.10.10.1` — a GL.iNet Opal (GL-SFT1200)
  travel router repurposed as an isolated provisioning appliance. Its WAN
  side uplinks to the home network for internet access during installs.
  Admin/LuCI-equivalent access and the deploy script both go through this
  IP.
- This is a deliberately isolated subnet, not the user's main home LAN.
  Nothing about "reach the hosts from my laptop on the main network" is
  solved yet — that's a known open item, not an oversight.

### Provisioning pipeline (bare-metal/)

```
bare-metal/
├── hosts.csv                          # hostname/MAC/IP source of truth
├── router/
│   ├── dnsmasq-provisioning.conf      # DHCP reservations + iPXE chainload
│   ├── boot.ipxe                      # MAC → kickstart dispatch
│   └── deploy-opal.sh                 # pushes config to the Opal over SSH
├── kickstart/
│   ├── ks-host1.cfg
│   ├── ks-host2.cfg
│   └── ks-host3.cfg
└── README.md                          # full write-up, read this for detail
```

Flow: host PXE-boots → Opal's dnsmasq recognizes its MAC and chainloads
iPXE → iPXE (`boot.ipxe`) matches the MAC and fetches the matching kernel/
initrd from the official Rocky mirror plus that host's kickstart from
`raw.githubusercontent.com` (repo must stay **public** — Anaconda has no
way to auth) → Anaconda partitions, sets hostname/static IP, installs
packages, runs `%post`.

Two things that bite people working on this pipeline:

1. **UEFI vs BIOS PXE binaries.** All three hosts are UEFI. The Opal serves
   `snponly.efi` (saved locally as `ipxe.efi`), not `undionly.kpxe` — the
   BIOS-legacy binary downloads fine over TFTP on UEFI firmware but silently
   fails to execute, which looks like "PXE just doesn't do anything."
2. **dnsmasq confdir is tmpfs.** On this firmware, `/tmp/dnsmasq.d` is
   wiped on every reboot. The real config lives in
   `/etc/dnsmasq.d/provisioning.conf` and gets re-mirrored into
   `/tmp/dnsmasq.d` by an `/etc/rc.local` hook. Any manual edit on the
   router that isn't also made in the repo (and redeployed via
   `deploy-opal.sh`) will disappear on next reboot.

Redeploying after any change to `router/*`: `./bare-metal/router/deploy-opal.sh 10.10.10.1`.

Full narrative and troubleshooting history: `bare-metal/README.md`.

### What's NOT built yet

Kubernetes itself has not been bootstrapped on this fleet. The repo still
contains `ansible/`, `terraform/proxmox/`, and `clusters/homelab/` (ArgoCD)
trees from the original Proxmox+VM design — they're aspirational/unused
right now, not a description of a running cluster. Concretely:

- `terraform/proxmox/` — no Proxmox host exists anymore to provision VMs on.
- `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml` — still needs to be pointed at the bare-metal
  IPs (`10.10.10.10/20/30`) instead of the old VM IPs before it's usable.
- No containerd/kubeadm/Cilium/MetalLB/Longhorn/ArgoCD has actually been
  installed on host1/2/3 yet.

If asked to bootstrap Kubernetes on this fleet, treat it as new work on top
of bare-metal Rocky hosts, not as "fix the existing cluster." Ansible's
roles (`common`, `containerd`, `kubeadm`, `control-plane`, `worker`) are
still a reasonable starting point in spirit, but the inventory needs fixing
first and everything should be validated against real hosts, not assumed
working.

### History (why bare-metal, not Proxmox)

The repo was originally templated for Proxmox VE on every node with K8s
running in VMs. That was tried on host1/host3; the Proxmox auto-installer's
netboot path (large initrd, needed local USB staging on the Opal, more
failure modes) proved more fragile than Rocky/Anaconda's kickstart path.
All three hosts were consolidated onto bare-metal Rocky Linux 9 instead —
simpler, and the PXE pipeline above is fully IaC-driven with no local
staging on the Opal's 128MB flash. Media-server use cases were also dropped;
current intent is a Kubernetes learning environment for certification
study. A later idea to swap Rocky for Talos OS was considered and shelved
("on reste sur Rocky pour le moment") — if it resurfaces, the previously
discussed topology preference was host3 (most RAM/CPU) as control-plane,
host1 + host2 as workers.

## Working conventions

- Repo: `github.com/maximepatry/k8s-homelab`, public (required for
  `raw.githubusercontent.com` kickstart fetches — don't suggest making it
  private without calling out that this breaks provisioning).
- Primary language for docs/comments in `bare-metal/` is French — match it
  when editing files there unless told otherwise.
- When you change host-facing config (kickstart, dnsmasq, boot.ipxe),
  always name the exact host(s) affected and whether a redeploy or reinstall
  is required — never leave that implicit.

# k8s-homelab

A self-hosted Kubernetes cluster running on bare-metal mini PCs, managed entirely with Infrastructure as Code.

## Hardware

| Node | Host | CPU | RAM | Role |
|------|------|-----|-----|------|
| `n150-cp` | Intel N150 | 3 vCPU | 10 GB | Control plane |
| `ser5-worker-1` | AMD Ryzen 5500U | 10 vCPU | 28 GB | Worker |
| `ser5-worker-2` | AMD Ryzen 5500U | 10 vCPU | 28 GB | Worker |

> Table above is the original template target (Proxmox + VMs). Actual
> current fleet is 3 bare-metal Rocky Linux 9 hosts (host1/host2/host3),
> no hypervisor anywhere - see the Note below.

## Stack

| Layer | Technology |
|-------|-----------|
| Hypervisor | ~~Proxmox VE~~ none - bare-metal (see Note below) |
| OS | Rocky Linux 9 (kickstart, bare-metal) |
| Container runtime | containerd |
| Kubernetes | kubeadm 1.31 |
| CNI | Cilium (eBPF) |
| Load balancer | MetalLB (L2) |
| Ingress | ingress-nginx |
| Storage | Longhorn |
| TLS | cert-manager |
| GitOps | ArgoCD (app-of-apps) |
| IaC | Terraform + Ansible |

## Repository Layout

```
.
├── bare-metal/             # PXE provisioning via a GL.iNet Opal (Rocky kickstart, all 3 hosts)
│   ├── router/             # GL.iNet Opal config (dnsmasq DHCP/TFTP + iPXE chainload)
│   └── kickstart/          # Rocky Linux 9 kickstarts, one per host
├── terraform/proxmox/      # Provision VMs on Proxmox (currently unused - see Note)
├── ansible/                # Bootstrap OS and kubeadm
│   ├── inventory/
│   ├── group_vars/
│   ├── playbooks/
│   └── roles/              # common, containerd, kubeadm, control-plane, worker
├── clusters/homelab/
│   ├── bootstrap/          # ArgoCD install + app-of-apps root Application
│   └── infrastructure/     # ArgoCD Application manifests (cilium, metallb, …)
├── apps/                   # User workloads (ArgoCD Applications)
├── monitoring/             # Observability stack
└── docs/                   # Detailed runbooks
```

> **Note**: this repo's stack was designed for Proxmox VE on every node with
> K8s running in VMs (Terraform provisions the VMs, Ansible bootstraps
> kubeadm inside them). The actual fleet ended up fully bare-metal instead -
> `host1`, `host2`, `host3` all run Rocky Linux 9 directly, provisioned via
> [`bare-metal/`](bare-metal/) (PXE + kickstart through a GL.iNet Opal, no
> hypervisor, no VMs). We tried Proxmox on host1/host3 first but the
> Proxmox auto-installer's netboot path (huge initrd, needs local USB
> staging on the Opal, more failure modes) turned out more fragile than
> Rocky/Anaconda's - see `bare-metal/README.md` for the full story.
>
> Practical consequence: `terraform/proxmox/` is currently unused - there's
> no Proxmox host left to provision VMs on. `ansible/` still applies in
> spirit (containerd + kubeadm bootstrap), but its `inventory/hosts.yml`
> and any Proxmox-specific assumptions need to point at the 3 bare-metal
> IPs (`10.10.10.10/20/30` on the provisioning subnet, or wherever they
> end up on the main LAN) instead of VM IPs. Not yet done.

## Getting Started

Provisioning goes through three stages: Proxmox → Terraform → Ansible → ArgoCD.

### 1. Proxmox

Follow [`docs/proxmox-setup.md`](docs/proxmox-setup.md) to:
- Install Proxmox VE on each node
- Create the Terraform API user
- Build the Rocky Linux 9 cloud-init template on each node

### 2. Terraform — provision VMs

```bash
cd terraform/proxmox
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars
# Fill in your Proxmox endpoints, credentials, and SSH key
terraform init
terraform apply
```

See [`docs/terraform.md`](docs/terraform.md) for variable reference.

### 3. Ansible — bootstrap Kubernetes

```bash
cd ansible
# Verify SSH connectivity
ansible -i inventory/hosts.yml all -m ping

# Bootstrap the full cluster
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.yml playbooks/bootstrap.yml
```

This installs containerd, kubeadm, initialises the control plane, and joins the workers.

See [`docs/ansible.md`](docs/ansible.md) for details.

### 4. ArgoCD — GitOps bootstrap

```bash
export KUBECONFIG=clusters/homelab/kubeconfig

# Install ArgoCD
kubectl create namespace argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
kubectl -n argocd wait --for=condition=available deploy/argocd-server --timeout=120s

# Set your repo URL in the file, then apply
kubectl apply -f clusters/homelab/bootstrap/app-of-apps.yml
```

ArgoCD will automatically deploy Cilium, MetalLB, Longhorn, cert-manager, and ingress-nginx.

> Sync Cilium first and wait for nodes to be `Ready` before syncing the remaining apps.

See [`docs/argocd-gitops.md`](docs/argocd-gitops.md) for the full bootstrap flow and day-2 operations.

## Network

```
LAN: 192.168.1.0/24

Proxmox hosts:  .10 / .11 / .12
K8s VMs:        .101 (cp) / .102 (worker-1) / .103 (worker-2)

Ingress path:
  LAN → MetalLB IP (L2 ARP) → ingress-nginx → Pods
                                    (eBPF observed by Cilium/Hubble)
```

See [`docs/networking.md`](docs/networking.md) for MetalLB IP pool and Cilium configuration.

## Documentation

| Doc | Contents |
|-----|----------|
| [`bare-metal/README.md`](bare-metal/README.md) | PXE/kickstart provisioning for bare-metal nodes via the GL.iNet Opal |
| [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) | Full architecture diagrams |
| [`docs/proxmox-setup.md`](docs/proxmox-setup.md) | Manual Proxmox prep steps |
| [`docs/terraform.md`](docs/terraform.md) | Terraform variable reference |
| [`docs/ansible.md`](docs/ansible.md) | Ansible roles and playbook details |
| [`docs/argocd-gitops.md`](docs/argocd-gitops.md) | GitOps workflow and ArgoCD usage |
| [`docs/networking.md`](docs/networking.md) | CNI, MetalLB, and ingress setup |
| [`docs/storage.md`](docs/storage.md) | Longhorn storage configuration |
| [`docs/day2-operations.md`](docs/day2-operations.md) | Upgrades, backups, common ops |

result.output:
# bare-metal-hmlab

Provisioning automatisé du homelab sur mini PC, via un GL.iNet Opal
(GL-SFT1200) en réseau de provisioning isolé, sans clé USB.

Fleet actuelle : **host1, host2, host3 - tous en Rocky Linux 9**, via
kickstart. Simplifié depuis une approche mixte Proxmox/Rocky qui s'est
avérée plus fragile (installeur Proxmox plus gros, dépendance à une clé
USB sur l'Opal, etc.) - Rocky/Anaconda est plus simple et plus fiable à
netbooter.

## Comment ça marche

1. L'Opal est reconfiguré en routeur isolé (LAN `10.10.10.0/24`, WAN uplinké
   vers le réseau domestique pour l'accès internet pendant l'install).
2. Le host boote en PXE (à activer dans son BIOS/UEFI).
3. `dnsmasq` sur l'Opal reconnaît chaque mini PC par adresse MAC
   (réservations statiques dans `router/dnsmasq-provisioning.conf`,
   source de vérité : `hosts.csv`) et chaîne vers iPXE.
4. iPXE (`router/boot.ipxe`) route par MAC vers le bon kickstart, puis va
   chercher le kernel/initrd Rocky et le kickstart directement en HTTPS
   (mirror officiel Rocky + ce repo GitHub) - rien de volumineux stocké
   sur les 128MB de flash de l'Opal, aucune clé USB nécessaire.
5. Anaconda installe selon le kickstart correspondant : partitionnement,
   hostname, IP statique, paquets, post-install.

## Après une install réussie : retirer le host du dispatch PXE

Le boot PXE lui-même ne redéclenche pas une réinstall à chaque reboot — un
firmware normal essaie le disque local en premier et ne retombe sur le
réseau que si le disque ne fournit aucun bootloader valide (ou si tu forces
un boot réseau ponctuel, ex. `efibootmgr -n`). Mais `boot.ipxe` n'a aucune
protection "skip si déjà installé" : si un host retombe un jour sur PXE
(ordre de boot mal configuré, disque en panne, etc.), il se refait wiper
sans prévenir. C'est exactement ce qui est arrivé à host2 (boucle
install/reboot/reinstall) avant qu'on corrige son ordre de boot BIOS.

Une fois qu'un host est confirmé opérationnel, retire son entrée du
pipeline. Deux options :

- **Supprimer** la ligne `dhcp-host=...` et le bloc `iseq .../:hostX` -
  plus propre si le host part pour de bon.
- **Commenter** (`#` devant la ligne `dhcp-host=...` dans
  `dnsmasq-provisioning.conf`, et devant la ligne
  `iseq ${mac} ... && goto hostX ||` dans `boot.ipxe`) - recommandé si tu
  comptes réactiver plus tard : ça évite de retaper/retrouver la MAC, tu
  décommentes juste la ligne. Le bloc `:hostX` (kernel/initrd/boot) peut
  rester tel quel dans les deux cas - une fois que rien ne saute dessus
  (`goto hostX`), il est inerte. C'est l'approche utilisée pour host2 en ce
  moment (déjà installé, dispatch commenté dans `boot.ipxe` uniquement -
  sa réservation `dhcp-host` reste active puisque c'est juste une IP pin,
  pas un déclencheur PXE).

Dans les deux cas, relance `./router/deploy-opal.sh <ip-de-l-opal>` pour
pousser le changement. Le host tombera alors dans le cas `:unknown` (shell
iPXE, pas d'install) s'il retente un PXE boot par accident.

## Structure

- `hosts.csv` - mapping hostname / MAC / IP pour les 3 hosts
- `router/dnsmasq-provisioning.conf` - DHCP + réservations + chainload iPXE
- `router/boot.ipxe` - menu de boot iPXE, dispatch par MAC
- `router/deploy-opal.sh` - déploie la config sur l'Opal via SSH
- `kickstart/ks-host{1,2,3}.cfg` - un kickstart Rocky par host

## À faire avant de lancer

- Remplacer la clé SSH placeholder dans chaque `kickstart/ks-hostX.cfg`
  si tu changes de clé (actuellement déjà remplie avec la clé utilisée
  pour host2)
- Reconfigurer le LAN de l'Opal en `10.10.10.1/24` (LuCI ou `uci`) - fait
- Activer le boot PXE dans le BIOS/UEFI de chaque host, et vérifier que le
  disque local reste prioritaire dans l'ordre de boot une fois l'install
  terminée (sinon boucle de réinstall - voir section précédente)

## Déploiement

```
./router/deploy-opal.sh <ip-de-l-opal>
```

Le script vérifie l'espace disque libre sur l'Opal, installe `dnsmasq-full`
si besoin, récupère le binaire iPXE (`snponly.efi`, build UEFI natif - voir
note ci-dessous), et pousse la config + `boot.ipxe`.

**Note UEFI vs BIOS legacy** : tous les hosts ici bootent en UEFI pur
(confirmé via leurs entrées `efibootmgr` type `UEFI: PXE IPv4 ...`). On
sert donc `snponly.efi` (build iPXE natif UEFI, réutilise le driver réseau
déjà initialisé par le firmware) plutôt que `undionly.kpxe` (BIOS legacy) -
ce dernier se télécharge très bien par TFTP mais un firmware UEFI ne peut
pas l'exécuter, et retombe silencieusement sur l'entrée de boot suivante
sans afficher d'erreur. C'est ce qui a fait perdre pas mal de temps sur le
debug de host3 au départ.

**Note firmware dnsmasq** : sur ce GL-SFT1200, `confdir` est réglé sur
`/tmp/dnsmasq.d` (tmpfs, effacé à chaque reboot). Le script garde donc la
copie de référence dans `/etc/dnsmasq.d/provisioning.conf` (persistant) et
la remiroir dans `/tmp/dnsmasq.d` à chaque démarrage via un hook
`/etc/rc.local`. Si tu modifies `dnsmasq-provisioning.conf` plus tard,
relance simplement `deploy-opal.sh` pour repousser la mise à jour.

`scp` ne fonctionne pas sur ce firmware (pas de serveur SFTP) - le script
utilise `ssh ... "cat > fichier" < local` à la place.

## Mise à jour de WireGuard sur l'Opal

Deux voies concrètes :

1. **Firmware officiel** : GL.iNet publie régulièrement des mises à jour
   pour le SFT1200 (dl.gl-inet.com/router/sft1200) incluant des correctifs
   liés à WireGuard - à vérifier/appliquer en premier, c'est le chemin le
   plus simple.
2. **SDK GL.iNet** (github.com/gl-inet/sdk) : le SFT1200/SF1200 utilise la
   target `siflower-1806`. Ça permet de recompiler `wireguard-tools` /
   `kmod-wireguard` contre le kernel exact de l'Opal et d'installer le
   `.ipk` résultant via `opkg` - un `opkg upgrade` simple ne suffit pas ici
   car le module kernel doit matcher l'ABI du kernel en place.

À noter : le protocole WireGuard lui-même n'a pas eu de rupture de
compatibilité depuis sa sortie - un module plus ancien reste tout à fait
interopérable avec des pairs récents. Mettre à jour apporte surtout des
correctifs de sécurité et des améliorations d'outillage, pas de la
connectivité en plus.

name: Deploy

# Rolling/release pipeline — manually triggered.
# Requires the self-hosted runner on the homelab.
# After Terraform and Ansible complete, ArgoCD is already watching the git repo
# and will roll out any manifest changes automatically. This job waits for that
# sync to confirm the cluster is fully converged before marking the run green.

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      target:
        description: "What to deploy"
        required: true
        default: all
        type: choice
        options:
          - terraform
          - ansible
          - all
      ansible_tags:
        description: "Ansible tags (e.g. containerd, kubeadm) — blank = full playbook"
        required: false
        default: ""
      dry_run:
        description: "Dry-run (plan/check only, no changes applied)"
        required: false
        default: "false"
        type: choice
        options:
          - "false"
          - "true"

jobs:
  terraform-apply:
    name: Terraform apply
    runs-on: [self-hosted, homelab]
    if: inputs.target == 'terraform' || inputs.target == 'all'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with:
          terraform_version: "~1.9"

      - name: Init
        run: terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox init
        env:
          TF_VAR_proxmox_password: ${{ secrets.PROXMOX_PASSWORD }}

      - name: Plan
        run: terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox plan -no-color -out=tfplan
        env:
          TF_VAR_proxmox_endpoint: ${{ secrets.PROXMOX_ENDPOINT }}
          TF_VAR_proxmox_password: ${{ secrets.PROXMOX_PASSWORD }}
          TF_VAR_ssh_public_key: ${{ secrets.SSH_PUBLIC_KEY }}

      - name: Apply
        if: inputs.dry_run == 'false'
        run: terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox apply -auto-approve tfplan
        env:
          TF_VAR_proxmox_endpoint: ${{ secrets.PROXMOX_ENDPOINT }}
          TF_VAR_proxmox_password: ${{ secrets.PROXMOX_PASSWORD }}
          TF_VAR_ssh_public_key: ${{ secrets.SSH_PUBLIC_KEY }}

  ansible-run:
    name: Ansible playbook
    runs-on: [self-hosted, homelab]
    needs: [terraform-apply]
    if: |
      always() &&
      !cancelled() &&
      (inputs.target == 'ansible' || inputs.target == 'all') &&
      (needs.terraform-apply.result == 'success' || needs.terraform-apply.result == 'skipped')
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run playbook
        run: |
          CMD="ansible-playbook -i ansible/inventory/hosts.yml ansible/playbooks/bootstrap.yml"
          if [ -n "${{ inputs.ansible_tags }}" ]; then
            CMD="$CMD --tags ${{ inputs.ansible_tags }}"
          fi
          if [ "${{ inputs.dry_run }}" = "true" ]; then
            CMD="$CMD --check --diff"
          fi
          $CMD
        env:
          ANSIBLE_FORCE_COLOR: "1"

  argocd-verify:
    name: Verify ArgoCD sync
    runs-on: [self-hosted, homelab]
    needs: [terraform-apply, ansible-run]
    if: |
      always() &&
      !cancelled() &&
      inputs.dry_run == 'false' &&
      (needs.ansible-run.result == 'success' || needs.ansible-run.result == 'skipped') &&
      (needs.terraform-apply.result == 'success' || needs.terraform-apply.result == 'skipped')
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Wait for ArgoCD to sync all apps
        run: |
          export KUBECONFIG="${HOME}/.kube/config"
          echo "Waiting up to 5 minutes for all ArgoCD apps to sync..."
          timeout 300 bash -c '
            until kubectl -n argocd get applications -o json \
              | jq -e "[.items[] | select(.metadata.name != \"app-of-apps\") | .status.sync.status] | length > 0 and all(. == \"Synced\")" \
              > /dev/null 2>&1; do
              echo "  still waiting... ($(kubectl -n argocd get applications --no-headers 2>/dev/null | awk "{print \$2}" | sort | uniq -c | tr -s " " | sed "s/^ //"))"
              sleep 15
            done
          '
          echo "All apps synced. Checking health..."
          kubectl -n argocd get applications

      - name: Assert all apps healthy
        run: |
          export KUBECONFIG="${HOME}/.kube/config"
          UNHEALTHY=$(kubectl -n argocd get applications -o json \
            | jq -r '.items[] | select(.status.health.status != "Healthy") | .metadata.name')
          if [ -n "$UNHEALTHY" ]; then
            echo "Unhealthy apps: $UNHEALTHY"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "All apps are Synced and Healthy."

name: Plan

# Terraform plan and Ansible dry-run on PRs and main pushes.
# Requires the self-hosted runner on the homelab (needs LAN access to Proxmox).
# See docs/ci-cd.md for runner setup instructions.

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "terraform/**"
      - "ansible/**"
  push:

    paths:
      - "terraform/**"
      - "ansible/**"

jobs:
  terraform-plan:
    name: Terraform plan
    runs-on: [self-hosted, homelab]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with:
          terraform_version: "~1.9"
          terraform_wrapper: true

      - name: Init
        run: terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox init
        env:
          TF_VAR_proxmox_password: ${{ secrets.PROXMOX_PASSWORD }}

      - name: Plan
        id: plan
        run: terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox plan -no-color -out=tfplan
        env:
          TF_VAR_proxmox_endpoint: ${{ secrets.PROXMOX_ENDPOINT }}
          TF_VAR_proxmox_password: ${{ secrets.PROXMOX_PASSWORD }}
          TF_VAR_ssh_public_key: ${{ secrets.SSH_PUBLIC_KEY }}
        continue-on-error: true

      - name: Comment plan on PR
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const plan = `${{ steps.plan.outputs.stdout }}`;
            const status = '${{ steps.plan.outcome }}' === 'success' ? '✅' : '❌';
            const body = `#### Terraform Plan ${status}
            <details><summary>Show plan</summary>

            \`\`\`hcl
            ${plan.slice(0, 60000)}
            \`\`\`

            </details>
            *Pushed by @${{ github.actor }}, action: \`${{ github.event_name }}\`*`;

            const { data: comments } = await github.rest.issues.listComments({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
            });
            const existing = comments.find(c =>
              c.user.type === 'Bot' && c.body.includes('Terraform Plan')
            );
            if (existing) {
              await github.rest.issues.updateComment({
                owner: context.repo.owner,
                repo: context.repo.repo,
                comment_id: existing.id,
                body,
              });
            } else {
              await github.rest.issues.createComment({
                owner: context.repo.owner,
                repo: context.repo.repo,
                issue_number: context.issue.number,
                body,
              });
            }

      - name: Fail if plan failed
        if: steps.plan.outcome == 'failure'
        run: exit 1

      - name: Upload plan artifact
        if: steps.plan.outcome == 'success'
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: tfplan-${{ github.sha }}
          path: terraform/proxmox/tfplan
          retention-days: 1

  ansible-check:
    name: Ansible dry-run
    runs-on: [self-hosted, homelab]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Check mode (no changes applied)
        run: |
          ansible-playbook \
            -i ansible/inventory/hosts.yml \
            ansible/playbooks/bootstrap.yml \
            --check --diff
        env:
          ANSIBLE_FORCE_COLOR: "1"

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Before touching anything infrastructure-related

Load the `homelab-engineer` skill (`.claude/skills/homelab-engineer/SKILL.md`) for any task that touches
provisioning, hosts, the router, or IPs/MACs. It has the current, verified ground truth (fleet inventory,
network layout, SSH access, PXE hazards). Do **not** trust `.claude/commands/homelab-context.md` /
`homelab-devops.md` (already deleted from this checkout but may reappear in old branches/PRs) or the
hardware table at the top of `README.md` for infra facts — both describe an earlier Proxmox+VM design
that was abandoned. `bare-metal/hosts.csv` is the single source of truth for hostname/MAC/IP.

## Repository structure — two very different halves

This repo currently contains two unrelated generations of the same project. Know which one a file
belongs to before editing it:

1. **`bare-metal/`** — the real, currently-live provisioning pipeline. Three mini PCs (host1/host2/host3)
   PXE-boot through a GL.iNet Opal router (dnsmasq + iPXE) straight into a Rocky Linux 9 kickstart install,
   no hypervisor. This is actively deployed and has real hardware behind it — treat changes here as
   production changes. See `bare-metal/README.md` (written in French, matches the rest of that directory)
   for the full flow, and the homelab-engineer skill for the PXE-reinstall hazard before editing
   `boot.ipxe` or `dnsmasq-provisioning.conf`.
2. **`terraform/proxmox/`, `ansible/`, `clusters/homelab/`, `apps/`, `infrastructure/`, `monitoring/`** —
   the original Proxmox VE + Terraform + kubeadm + ArgoCD design. Proxmox was abandoned in favor of the
   bare-metal approach above, so **none of this is deployed** — no Kubernetes cluster exists anywhere on
   the fleet yet. `apps/`, `infrastructure/`, and `monitoring/` are currently empty placeholder
   directories. `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml` still points at the old VM IPs (`192.168.1.101-103`), not
   the real hosts (`10.10.10.10/20/30`) — fix that before any Ansible run is expected to work. Treat work
   in this half as new development against real bare-metal hosts, not as "fixing" a working cluster.

`docs/*.md` (architecture, terraform, ansible, argocd-gitops, networking, storage, day2-operations)
document the aspirational Proxmox/K8s design in half 2, not the current bare-metal-only reality — useful
for the target design, not for what's actually running.

## Commands

CI (`.github/workflows/validate.yml`) runs these on every push/PR; run them locally before committing
changes under `terraform/` or `ansible/`:

```bash
# Terraform (terraform/proxmox)
terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox fmt -check -recursive
terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox init -backend=false
terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox validate

# Ansible lint (config: .ansible-lint, basic profile)
ANSIBLE_ROLES_PATH=ansible/roles ansible-lint ansible/

# YAML lint (config: .yamllint.yml — 150-col limit, Ansible yes/no truthy allowed)
yamllint -c .yamllint.yml clusters/ ansible/
```

`plan.yml` and `deploy.yml` (Terraform plan/apply, Ansible bootstrap, ArgoCD sync verification) require
the self-hosted `[self-hosted, homelab]` GitHub Actions runner with LAN access to Proxmox — they won't run
on a normal machine and are moot until half 2 above is actually stood up.

Redeploying the bare-metal provisioning pipeline after any change under `bare-metal/router/`:

```bash
./bare-metal/router/deploy-opal.sh 10.10.10.1
```

There is no equivalent local validation for `bare-metal/kickstart/*.cfg` or `bare-metal/router/boot.ipxe` —
they're only exercised by an actual PXE boot, so review changes carefully (especially MAC dispatch in
`boot.ipxe`, which has no "already installed" guard).

## Working conventions

- Repo must stay **public** — Anaconda fetches kickstarts from `raw.githubusercontent.com` with no auth
  path. Don't suggest making it private without flagging that this breaks provisioning.
- `bare-metal/` docs and comments are in French; match that when editing files there.
- When changing host-facing config (kickstart, dnsmasq, boot.ipxe), always state which host(s) are
  affected and whether the change requires a redeploy (`deploy-opal.sh`) or a full reinstall.

    state: absent

- name: Disable zram-generator (Rocky Linux 9 swap via zram)
  systemd:
    name: "{{ item }}"
    enabled: false
    state: stopped
    masked: true
  loop:
    - swap.target
  ignore_errors: true

- name: Load required kernel modules
  modprobe:
    name: "{{ item }}"
    state: present
  loop:
    - overlay
    - br_netfilter

- name: Persist kernel modules
  copy:
    dest: /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
    content: |
      overlay
      br_netfilter

- name: Set sysctl params for k8s networking
  sysctl:
    name: "{{ item.key }}"
    value: "{{ item.value }}"
    sysctl_file: /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
    reload: true
  loop:
    - { key: net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables,  value: "1" }
    - { key: net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables, value: "1" }
    - { key: net.ipv4.ip_forward,                 value: "1" }

# firewalld is enabled by default on Rocky — disable it; Cilium manages eBPF rules
- name: Disable firewalld
  systemd:
    name: firewalld
    enabled: false
    state: stopped
  ignore_errors: true

- name: Set SELinux to permissive
  selinux:
    policy: targeted
    state: permissive

- name: Persist SELinux permissive
  replace:
    path: /etc/selinux/config
    regexp: '^SELINUX=enforcing'
    replace: 'SELINUX=permissive'

---
- name: Add Docker CE repo (provides containerd.io for Rocky)
  get_url:
    url: https://download.docker.com/linux/centos/docker-ce.repo
    dest: /etc/yum.repos.d/docker-ce.repo

- name: Install containerd
  dnf:
    name: "containerd.io"
    state: present

- name: Create containerd config directory
  file:
    path: /etc/containerd

- name: Generate default containerd config
  shell: containerd config default > /etc/containerd/config.toml
  args:
    creates: /etc/containerd/config.toml

- name: Enable SystemdCgroup in containerd
  replace:
    path: /etc/containerd/config.toml

- name: Enable and start containerd

---
- name: Add Kubernetes repo
  copy:
    dest: /etc/yum.repos.d/kubernetes.repo
    content: |
      [kubernetes]
      name=Kubernetes
      baseurl=https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v{{ kubernetes_version }}/rpm/
      enabled=1
      gpgcheck=1
      gpgkey=https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v{{ kubernetes_version }}/rpm/repodata/repomd.xml.key
      exclude=kubelet kubeadm kubectl cri-tools kubernetes-cni

- name: Install kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl

    name:
      - kubelet
      - kubeadm
      - kubectl
    state: present
    disable_excludes: kubernetes

- name: Hold kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl (dnf versionlock)
  command: dnf versionlock add {{ item }}
  loop:
    - kubelet
    - kubeadm
    - kubectl
  changed_when: false

- name: Enable kubelet

---
- name: Check if cluster is already initialized
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
  register: kubeadm_conf

- name: Initialize cluster with kubeadm
  command: >
    kubeadm init
    --pod-network-cidr={{ pod_cidr }}
    --service-cidr={{ service_cidr }}
    --cluster-name={{ cluster_name }}
    --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy
  when: not kubeadm_conf.stat.exists
  register: kubeadm_init

# skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy because Cilium replaces kube-proxy

- name: Create .kube directory for rocky user
  file:
    path: /home/rocky/.kube
    state: directory
    owner: rocky
    group: rocky

- name: Copy admin kubeconfig
  copy:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: /home/rocky/.kube/config
    remote_src: true
    owner: rocky
    group: rocky
    mode: "0600"

- name: Fetch kubeconfig to local machine
  fetch:
    src: /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
    dest: "{{ playbook_dir }}/../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig"
    flat: true

- name: Generate join command
  command: kubeadm token create --print-join-command
  register: join_command
  changed_when: false

- name: Store join command for workers
  set_fact:
    kubeadm_join_command: "{{ join_command.stdout }}"
  delegate_to: localhost
  delegate_facts: true
=== ansible/roles/worker/tasks/main.yml ===
---
- name: Check if node is already joined
  stat:
    path: /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf
  register: kubelet_conf

- name: Join cluster
  command: "{{ hostvars['localhost']['kubeadm_join_command'] }}"
  when: not kubelet_conf.stat.exists

- name: Label node as worker
  command: >
    kubectl --kubeconfig /home/ubuntu/.kube/config
    label node {{ inventory_hostname }} node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=worker --overwrite
  delegate_to: "{{ groups['control_plane'][0] }}"
  become: false

---networking---
# Networking

## Cilium (CNI)

Cilium replaces both the CNI plugin and kube-proxy. It uses eBPF for packet processing instead of iptables.

### Why kube-proxy is absent

`kubeadm init` was run with `--skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy`. There is **no kube-proxy DaemonSet** in this cluster. If you look for it you won't find it — this is expected.

Cilium is deployed with `kubeProxyReplacement: true`, which activates its full service routing stack. All `ClusterIP`, `NodePort`, and `LoadBalancer` traffic is handled by Cilium's eBPF programs.

### Hubble (observability)

Hubble is enabled and provides network flow visibility:

```bash
# CLI (install hubble CLI: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/observability/hubble/setup/)
hubble observe --follow
hubble observe --namespace my-namespace
hubble observe --pod my-pod --verdict DROPPED

# UI (port-forward)
kubectl -n kube-system port-forward svc/hubble-ui 12000:80
# Open http://localhost:12000
```

### Checking Cilium health

```bash
# Summary
cilium status

# Full connectivity test (creates test pods, verifies pod-to-pod, pod-to-svc, etc.)
cilium connectivity test

# From inside a Cilium pod
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg endpoint list
```

### Network Policies

Cilium enforces standard Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` resources and its own extended `CiliumNetworkPolicy` CRD, which supports L7 policies (HTTP, gRPC, DNS).

---

## MetalLB (LoadBalancer)

MetalLB runs in **L2 mode**, which means it responds to ARP requests for LoadBalancer IPs on behalf of the cluster. No BGP router is needed.

### Required post-Helm CRs

The Helm chart installs the MetalLB controller and speaker but does **not** create an IP pool. You must apply these manually after Helm deploys MetalLB:

```yaml
# infrastructure/metallb/ip-address-pool.yml
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: homelab-pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 192.168.1.200-192.168.1.220   # adjust to a free range on your LAN
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: L2Advertisement
metadata:
  name: homelab-l2
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - homelab-pool
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f infrastructure/metallb/ip-address-pool.yml
```

### Verifying

```bash
kubectl get ipaddresspool,l2advertisement -n metallb-system
kubectl get svc -A | grep LoadBalancer
```

If a `LoadBalancer` service is stuck in `<pending>`, `IPAddressPool` is missing or has no free IPs.

### IP range planning

Pick a range outside your router's DHCP range to avoid conflicts. Example with a typical home router DHCP pool of `192.168.1.2–192.168.1.150`:

```
MetalLB pool: 192.168.1.200–192.168.1.220
```

# --- Provisioning network config for GL-SFT1200 (Opal) ---
# Assumes the Opal's LAN has already been set to 10.10.10.1/24 via the
# GL.iNet admin UI (Router IP 10.10.10.1, DHCP range 10.10.10.2-249) -
# that part is done and managed via UCI, so this file does NOT redeclare
# `interface=` or `dhcp-range=` for br-lan (would conflict/duplicate with
# the UI-managed range). This file only adds what the UI can't: static
# MAC reservations and the PXE/iPXE chainload.
#
# On OpenWrt, this file is meant to be dropped where dnsmasq picks up extra
# config (commonly /etc/dnsmasq.d/*.conf if `confdir` is set on the dnsmasq
# UCI instance, e.g. `uci set dhcp.@dnsmasq[0].confdir='/etc/dnsmasq.d'`).
# Check `uci show dhcp` on the router first — GL.iNet firmware sometimes wires
# this differently; deploy-opal.sh checks for you.

# --- Static reservations (source of truth: hosts.csv) ---
# All three hosts are Rocky Linux 9 via kickstart. Reservations stay here
# regardless of whether a host currently has a boot.ipxe dispatch case -
# they're just IP pins, not PXE triggers (that's controlled separately in
# boot.ipxe, where host2 is commented out post-install).
dhcp-host=78:55:36:02:de:9e,10.10.10.10,host1,infinite
dhcp-host=e8:ff:1e:d8:a0:d0,10.10.10.20,host2,infinite
dhcp-host=00:16:96:ee:1e:4d,10.10.10.30,host3,infinite

# --- PXE / iPXE chainload ---
# Stage 1: PXE ROM only speaks TFTP -> serve the small iPXE binary.
# host2/host3 are both modern UEFI-only mini PCs (confirmed via their
# efibootmgr "UEFI: PXE IPv4 ..." boot entries), so we serve ipxe.efi
# (the UEFI-native build) rather than undionly.kpxe (BIOS/legacy-only -
# a UEFI firmware downloads it fine over TFTP but can't execute it, then
# silently falls through to the next boot entry - looks like "PXE did
# nothing" with zero error on screen).
# Stage 2: once the client IS iPXE (it tags itself via DHCP user-class
# "iPXE"), hand it a boot script over HTTP instead. This avoids storing the
# large Rocky vmlinuz/initrd.img on the Opal's 128MB flash - iPXE fetches
# those directly from the Rocky mirror and your GitHub repo over HTTPS.
enable-tftp
tftp-root=/www/ipxe

dhcp-boot=ipxe.efi,,10.10.10.1
dhcp-userclass=set:ipxe,iPXE
dhcp-boot=tag:ipxe,http://10.10.10.1/boot.ipxe

input.content:
# Reconcile the Proxmox-era IaC design with the real bare-metal fleet

## Context

This repo was originally scaffolded for Proxmox VE + Terraform (VM provisioning) + Ansible (kubeadm
bootstrap inside the VMs) + ArgoCD (GitOps). That design was abandoned — the fleet is now **3 bare-metal
Rocky Linux 9 hosts** (host1/host2/host3), provisioned via PXE/kickstart through a GL.iNet Opal, with no
hypervisor. `bare-metal/` (the provisioning half) is real and already working. Everything above the OS —
`terraform/proxmox/`, `ansible/`, `clusters/homelab/` — was written for VMs that no longer exist, and no
Kubernetes cluster has actually been bootstrapped yet.

The goal now: stand up a real k8s cluster on top of the 3 bare-metal hosts, with Terraform and Ansible
doing the bootstrap and ArgoCD owning day-2 GitOps, all driven by a pipeline, with a Mac laptop acting as
the jumpbox/config station (over a new WireGuard tunnel into the isolated `10.10.10.0/24` LAN, since the
Mac normally lives on the home network).

Decisions locked in for this plan (confirmed with you):
- **Terraform scope**: bootstrap-only. It installs ArgoCD (+ the root Application) onto the freshly
  kubeadm'd cluster, then GitOps owns Cilium/MetalLB/ingress/cert-manager/Longhorn/apps from there.
  `terraform/proxmox/` (VM provisioning) is retired — nothing left for it to provision.
- **GitOps tool**: ArgoCD, reusing/fixing the existing `clusters/homelab/` scaffold rather than building
  Flux from scratch.
- **Jumpbox network**: Mac stays on the home LAN day-to-day and reaches `10.10.10.0/24` through a new
  WireGuard tunnel terminating on the Opal.
- **CI**: a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner lives on the jumpbox (Mac), matching the `[self-hosted,
  homelab]` label the existing workflows already expect.
- **Topology** (per prior discussion recorded in the homelab-engineer skill): host3 (Ryzen 7 5800H,
  32GB — the beefiest) as the single control-plane node; host1 + host2 as workers.

Target end-to-end flow once this is done:
```
Mac (jumpbox, WireGuard) ──ssh──▶ host1/2/3 (10.10.10.10/20/30)
        │
        ├─ ansible-playbook bootstrap.yml   → containerd + kubeadm init (host3) + join (host1/host2)
        ├─ terraform apply (cluster-bootstrap) → installs ArgoCD + root Application via kubeconfig
        └─ ArgoCD syncs clusters/homelab/infrastructure/*  → Cilium, MetalLB, ingress-nginx, cert-manager, Longhorn
```

## 1. Jumpbox network access (WireGuard on the Opal)

- Before touching config, SSH to the Opal and check current state (`uci show network`, any existing
  `wireguard-*` interfaces/packages) — the Opal is a travel router and may already have WireGuard
  installed/used for something unrelated; don't assume a clean slate.
- Add a new WireGuard interface on the Opal (e.g. `wg-mgmt`) with a firewall rule allowing forwarding from
  that interface's zone into the `lan` zone (`10.10.10.0/24`), so tunnel traffic can actually reach the
  hosts — a bare WG interface without this forwarding rule will connect but not route.
- Generate keys **locally** (on the Mac and for the Opal side), never commit private keys — `.gitignore`
  already excludes `*.key`/`*.pem`/`secrets/`; keep the Opal's WG private key and the Mac's WG private key
  out of the repo entirely. What goes in the repo is the *shape* of the config (interface/firewall UCI
  commands, peer AllowedIPs), the same pattern `deploy-opal.sh` already uses for the rest of the router
  config.
- Add a `bare-metal/router/deploy-wireguard.sh` (or extend `deploy-opal.sh`) that pushes the UCI
  WireGuard/firewall config the same way the existing script pushes dnsmasq/boot.ipxe — keeps this
  IaC-driven instead of a one-off LuCI click-through that silently drifts.
- On the Mac: WireGuard client config with `AllowedIPs = 10.10.10.0/24`, endpoint = Opal's home-LAN/WAN
  address. Document in `bare-metal/README.md` (French, matching that directory) how to bring the tunnel up
  before running Ansible/Terraform/kubectl from the jumpbox.

## 2. Fix Ansible to actually target the bare-metal hosts

Current `ansible/` is close in spirit but was written against Proxmox-VM assumptions (`rocky`/`ubuntu`
users that don't exist here — kickstart creates `foo`, root is locked). Concrete fixes:

- `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml`: replace `n150-cp`/`ser5-worker-*` @ `192.168.1.10x` with `host3` @
  `10.10.10.30` under `control_plane`, `host1`/`host2` @ `10.10.10.10`/`10.10.10.20` under `workers`.
- `ansible/ansible.cfg`: `remote_user = rocky` → `foo`; `private_key_file` → `~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab`
  (the non-default key name the skill documents).
- `ansible/group_vars/all.yml`: `ansible_user: rocky` → `foo`.
- `ansible/roles/control-plane/tasks/main.yml`: `/home/rocky/.kube` → `/home/foo/.kube` (dir + kubeconfig
  copy + owner/group).
- `ansible/roles/worker/tasks/main.yml`: the "Label node as worker" task references
  `/home/ubuntu/.kube/config`, which was never even consistent with the control-plane role's `rocky` user
  — fix to `/home/foo/.kube/config`.
- The rest of `common`/`containerd`/`kubeadm` roles and `bootstrap.yml`'s structure (common → containerd →
  kubeadm on all nodes, then control-plane init, then worker join) are sound as-is — reuse them, don't
  rewrite.
- **Open item to verify before running the `worker` role's Longhorn bits**: `group_vars/workers.yml` sets
  `longhorn_data_disk: /dev/sdb`, inherited from a design where Proxmox attached a dedicated virtual data
  disk. Bare-metal mini PCs may only have a single NVMe/SSD. Check via `ssh foo@hostX lsblk` before
  assuming `/dev/sdb` exists — if there's no second disk, Longhorn needs to be pointed at a path on the
  root disk instead (`defaultDataPath` in its Helm values, set later in step 3/4) rather than a dedicated
  block device.
- Fetched kubeconfig destination (`clusters/homelab/kubeconfig`, written by the control-plane role's
  `fetch` task) is **not currently gitignored** — add it to `.gitignore` before running this against a
  public repo; the file is a live cluster-admin credential.

## 3. Replace `terraform/proxmox/` with a bootstrap-only module

Delete `terraform/proxmox/` (VM provisioning, `bpg/proxmox` provider — nothing left for it to target) and
add `terraform/cluster-bootstrap/`:

- **Providers**: `hashicorp/kubernetes` and `hashicorp/helm`, both configured via
  `config_path = var.kubeconfig_path` (default `../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig`, the file Ansible just
  fetched in step 2).
- **`helm_release "argocd"`**: installs the `argo-cd` chart (argoproj Helm repo) into a new `argocd`
  namespace (`create_namespace = true`) — replaces the current plain-manifest
  `clusters/homelab/bootstrap/argocd-install.yml` + the manual `kubectl apply` step documented in
  `docs/argocd-gitops.md`.
- **Root Application**: apply `clusters/homelab/bootstrap/app-of-apps.yml` as a `kubectl_manifest`
  resource (use the `alekc/kubectl` provider — handles CRDs that don't exist until the ArgoCD Helm release
  lands, which the core `kubernetes_manifest` resource doesn't handle cleanly) with

# Reconcile the Proxmox-era IaC design with the real bare-metal fleet

## Context

This repo was originally scaffolded for Proxmox VE + Terraform (VM provisioning) + Ansible (kubeadm
bootstrap inside the VMs) + ArgoCD (GitOps). That design was abandoned — the fleet is now **3 bare-metal
Rocky Linux 9 hosts** (host1/host2/host3), provisioned via PXE/kickstart through a GL.iNet Opal, with no
hypervisor. `bare-metal/` (the provisioning half) is real and already working. Everything above the OS —
`terraform/proxmox/`, `ansible/`, `clusters/homelab/` — was written for VMs that no longer exist, and no
Kubernetes cluster has actually been bootstrapped yet.

The goal now: stand up a real k8s cluster on top of the 3 bare-metal hosts, with Terraform and Ansible
doing the bootstrap and ArgoCD owning day-2 GitOps, all driven by a pipeline, with a Mac laptop acting as
the jumpbox/config station (over a new WireGuard tunnel into the isolated `10.10.10.0/24` LAN, since the
Mac normally lives on the home network).

Decisions locked in for this plan (confirmed with you):
- **Terraform scope**: bootstrap-only. It installs ArgoCD (+ the root Application) onto the freshly
  kubeadm'd cluster, then GitOps owns Cilium/MetalLB/ingress/cert-manager/Longhorn/apps from there.
  `terraform/proxmox/` (VM provisioning) is retired — nothing left for it to provision.
- **GitOps tool**: ArgoCD, reusing/fixing the existing `clusters/homelab/` scaffold rather than building
  Flux from scratch.
- **Jumpbox network**: Mac stays on the home LAN day-to-day and reaches `10.10.10.0/24` through a new
  WireGuard tunnel terminating on the Opal.
- **CI**: a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner lives on the jumpbox (Mac), matching the `[self-hosted,
  homelab]` label the existing workflows already expect.
- **Topology** (per prior discussion recorded in the homelab-engineer skill): host3 (Ryzen 7 5800H,
  32GB — the beefiest) as the single control-plane node; host1 + host2 as workers.

Target end-to-end flow once this is done:
```
Mac (jumpbox, WireGuard) ──ssh──▶ host1/2/3 (10.10.10.10/20/30)
        │
        ├─ ansible-playbook bootstrap.yml   → containerd + kubeadm init (host3) + join (host1/host2)
        ├─ terraform apply (cluster-bootstrap) → installs ArgoCD + root Application via kubeconfig
        └─ ArgoCD syncs clusters/homelab/infrastructure/*  → Cilium, MetalLB, ingress-nginx, cert-manager, Longhorn
```

  `wireguard-*` interfaces/packages) — the Opal is a travel router and may already have WireGuard
  installed/used for something unrelated; don't assume a clean slate.
- Add a new WireGuard interface on the Opal (e.g. `wg-mgmt`) with a firewall rule allowing forwarding from
  that interface's zone into the `lan` zone (`10.10.10.0/24`), so tunnel traffic can actually reach the
  hosts — a bare WG interface without this forwarding rule will connect but not route.
- Generate keys **locally** (on the Mac and for the Opal side), never commit private keys — `.gitignore`
  already excludes `*.key`/`*.pem`/`secrets/`; keep the Opal's WG private key and the Mac's WG private key
  out of the repo entirely. What goes in the repo is the *shape* of the config (interface/firewall UCI
  commands, peer AllowedIPs), the same pattern `deploy-opal.sh` already uses for the rest of the router
  config.

  WireGuard/firewall config the same way the existing script pushes dnsmasq/boot.ipxe — keeps this
  IaC-driven instead of a one-off LuCI click-through that silently drifts.

  before running Ansible/Terraform/kubectl from the jumpbox.

# Reconcile the Proxmox-era IaC design with the real bare-metal fleet

## Context

This repo was originally scaffolded for Proxmox VE + Terraform (VM provisioning) + Ansible (kubeadm
bootstrap inside the VMs) + ArgoCD (GitOps). That design was abandoned — the fleet is now **3 bare-metal
Rocky Linux 9 hosts** (host1/host2/host3), provisioned via PXE/kickstart through a GL.iNet Opal, with no
hypervisor. `bare-metal/` (the provisioning half) is real and already working. Everything above the OS —
`terraform/proxmox/`, `ansible/`, `clusters/homelab/` — was written for VMs that no longer exist, and no
Kubernetes cluster has actually been bootstrapped yet.

The goal now: stand up a real k8s cluster on top of the 3 bare-metal hosts, with Terraform and Ansible
doing the bootstrap and ArgoCD owning day-2 GitOps, all driven by a pipeline, with a Mac laptop acting as
the jumpbox/config station (over a new WireGuard tunnel into the isolated `10.10.10.0/24` LAN, since the
Mac normally lives on the home network).

Decisions locked in for this plan (confirmed with you):
- **Terraform scope**: bootstrap-only. It installs ArgoCD (+ the root Applications/AppProjects) onto the
  freshly kubeadm'd cluster, then GitOps owns Cilium/MetalLB/ingress/cert-manager/Longhorn/apps from there.
  `terraform/proxmox/` (VM provisioning) is retired — nothing left for it to provision.
- **GitOps tool**: ArgoCD, reusing/fixing the existing `clusters/homelab/` scaffold rather than building
  Flux from scratch.
- **Jumpbox network**: Mac stays on the home LAN day-to-day and reaches `10.10.10.0/24` through a new
  WireGuard tunnel terminating on the Opal.
- **CI**: a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner lives on the jumpbox (Mac), matching the `[self-hosted,
  homelab]` label the existing workflows already expect.
- **Prod/stage split**: one physical cluster, not two — separation happens in ArgoCD (two `AppProject`s,
  two namespaces: `prod`/`stage`), not at the kubeadm/host level. Rejected splitting the 3 hosts into two
  independent clusters as too thin on capacity/HA either way for a homelab this size.
- **Topology — corrected by live hardware polling** (see README hardware table, polled 2026-08-11): the
  homelab-engineer skill's note that "host3 is the beefiest" is **wrong** — host1 (Ryzen 7 6800H, 1TB NVMe)
  is actually the strongest node, host3 (Ryzen 7 5800H, 512GB) is mid-pack, host2 (Intel N150, 16GB) is
  clearly the lightest. Using that real data: **host1 = control-plane, host2 + host3 = workers.** The
  control-plane taint is removed post-init so host1's capacity isn't wasted on etcd alone — normal for a
  single-CP homelab cluster.

Target end-to-end flow once this is done:
```
Mac (jumpbox, WireGuard) ──ssh──▶ host1/2/3 (10.10.10.10/20/30)
        │
        ├─ ansible-playbook bootstrap.yml   → containerd + kubeadm init (host1) + join (host2/host3)
        ├─ terraform apply (cluster-bootstrap) → installs ArgoCD + AppProjects/root Apps via kubeconfig
        └─ ArgoCD syncs:
             clusters/homelab/infrastructure/*  → Cilium, MetalLB, ingress-nginx, cert-manager, Longhorn
             apps/prod/*   (AppProject "prod",  namespace prod)  → your prod workloads
             apps/stage/*  (AppProject "stage", namespace stage) → your stage workloads
```

## 1. Jumpbox network access (WireGuard on the Opal)

- Before touching config, SSH to the Opal and check current state (`uci show network`, any existing
  `wireguard-*` interfaces/packages) — the Opal is a travel router and may already have WireGuard
  installed/used for something unrelated; don't assume a clean slate.
- Add a new WireGuard interface on the Opal (e.g. `wg-mgmt`) with a firewall rule allowing forwarding from
  that interface's zone into the `lan` zone (`10.10.10.0/24`), so tunnel traffic can actually reach the
  hosts — a bare WG interface without this forwarding rule will connect but not route.
- Generate keys **locally** (on the Mac and for the Opal side), never commit private keys — `.gitignore`
  already excludes `*.key`/`*.pem`/`secrets/`; keep the Opal's WG private key and the Mac's WG private key
  out of the repo entirely. What goes in the repo is the *shape* of the config (interface/firewall UCI
  commands, peer AllowedIPs), the same pattern `deploy-opal.sh` already uses for the rest of the router
  config.
- Add a `bare-metal/router/deploy-wireguard.sh` (or extend `deploy-opal.sh`) that pushes the UCI
  WireGuard/firewall config the same way the existing script pushes dnsmasq/boot.ipxe — keeps this
  IaC-driven instead of a one-off LuCI click-through that silently drifts.
- On the Mac: WireGuard client config with `AllowedIPs = 10.10.10.0/24`, endpoint = Opal's home-LAN/WAN
  address. Document in `bare-metal/README.md` (French, matching that directory) how to bring the tunnel up
  before running Ansible/Terraform/kubectl from the jumpbox.

hypervisor. `bare-metal/` (the provisioning half) is real and already working. Everything above the OS —
`terraform/proxmox/`, `ansible/`, `clusters/homelab/` — was written for VMs that no longer exist, and no
Kubernetes cluster has actually been bootstrapped yet.

The goal now: stand up a real k8s cluster on top of the 3 bare-metal hosts, with Terraform and Ansible
doing the bootstrap and ArgoCD owning day-2 GitOps, all driven by a pipeline, with a Mac laptop acting as
the jumpbox/config station (over a new WireGuard tunnel into the isolated `10.10.10.0/24` LAN, since the
Mac normally lives on the home network).

Decisions locked in for this plan (confirmed with you):
- **Terraform scope**: bootstrap-only. It installs ArgoCD (+ the root Applications/AppProjects) onto the
  freshly kubeadm'd cluster, then GitOps owns Cilium/MetalLB/ingress/cert-manager/Longhorn/apps from there.
  `terraform/proxmox/` (VM provisioning) is retired — nothing left for it to provision.
- **GitOps tool**: ArgoCD, reusing/fixing the existing `clusters/homelab/` scaffold rather than building
  Flux from scratch.
- **Jumpbox network**: Mac stays on the home LAN day-to-day and reaches `10.10.10.0/24` through a new
  WireGuard tunnel terminating on the Opal.
- **CI**: a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner lives on the jumpbox (Mac), matching the `[self-hosted,
  homelab]` label the existing workflows already expect.
- **Prod/stage split**: one physical cluster, not two — separation happens in ArgoCD (two `AppProject`s,
  two namespaces: `prod`/`stage`), not at the kubeadm/host level. Rejected splitting the 3 hosts into two
  independent clusters as too thin on capacity/HA either way for a homelab this size.
- **Topology — corrected by live hardware polling** (see README hardware table, polled 2026-08-11): the
  homelab-engineer skill's note that "host3 is the beefiest" is **wrong** — host1 (Ryzen 7 6800H, 1TB NVMe)
  is actually the strongest node, host3 (Ryzen 7 5800H, 512GB) is mid-pack, host2 (Intel N150, 16GB) is
  clearly the lightest. Using that real data: **host1 = control-plane, host2 + host3 = workers.** The
  control-plane taint is removed post-init so host1's capacity isn't wasted on etcd alone — normal for a
  single-CP homelab cluster.

Target end-to-end flow once this is done:
```
Mac (jumpbox, WireGuard) ──ssh──▶ host1/2/3 (10.10.10.10/20/30)
        │
        ├─ ansible-playbook bootstrap.yml   → containerd + kubeadm init (host1) + join (host2/host3)
        ├─ terraform apply (cluster-bootstrap) → installs ArgoCD + AppProjects/root Apps via kubeconfig
        └─ ArgoCD syncs:
             clusters/homelab/infrastructure/*  → Cilium, MetalLB, ingress-nginx, cert-manager, Longhorn
             apps/prod/*   (AppProject "prod",  namespace prod)  → your prod workloads
             apps/stage/*  (AppProject "stage", namespace stage) → your stage workloads
```

## 1. Jumpbox network access (WireGuard on the Opal)

- Before touching config, SSH to the Opal and check current state (`uci show network`, any existing
  `wireguard-*` interfaces/packages) — the Opal is a travel router and may already have WireGuard
  installed/used for something unrelated; don't assume a clean slate.
- Add a new WireGuard interface on the Opal (e.g. `wg-mgmt`) with a firewall rule allowing forwarding from
  that interface's zone into the `lan` zone (`10.10.10.0/24`), so tunnel traffic can actually reach the
  hosts — a bare WG interface without this forwarding rule will connect but not route.
- Generate keys **locally** (on the Mac and for the Opal side), never commit private keys — `.gitignore`
  already excludes `*.key`/`*.pem`/`secrets/`; keep the Opal's WG private key and the Mac's WG private key
  out of the repo entirely. What goes in the repo is the *shape* of the config (interface/firewall UCI
  commands, peer AllowedIPs), the same pattern `deploy-opal.sh` already uses for the rest of the router
  config.
- Add a `bare-metal/router/deploy-wireguard.sh` (or extend `deploy-opal.sh`) that pushes the UCI
  WireGuard/firewall config the same way the existing script pushes dnsmasq/boot.ipxe — keeps this
  IaC-driven instead of a one-off LuCI click-through that silently drifts.
- On the Mac: WireGuard client config with `AllowedIPs = 10.10.10.0/24`, endpoint = Opal's home-LAN/WAN
  address. Document in `bare-metal/README.md` (French, matching that directory) how to bring the tunnel up
  before running Ansible/Terraform/kubectl from the jumpbox.

## 2. Fix Ansible to actually target the bare-metal hosts

Current `ansible/` is close in spirit but was written against Proxmox-VM assumptions (`rocky`/`ubuntu`
users that don't exist here — kickstart creates `foo`, root is locked). Concrete fixes:

- `ansible/inventory/hosts.yml`: replace `n150-cp`/`ser5-worker-*` @ `192.168.1.10x` with `host1` @
  `10.10.10.10` under `control_plane`, `host2`/`host3` @ `10.10.10.20`/`10.10.10.30` under `workers`
  (topology per the corrected hardware data above).
- `ansible/ansible.cfg`: `remote_user = rocky` → `foo`; `private_key_file` → `~/.ssh/id_ed25519_homelab`
  (the non-default key name the skill documents).
- `ansible/group_vars/all.yml`: `ansible_user: rocky` → `foo`.
- `ansible/roles/control-plane/tasks/main.yml`: `/home/rocky/.kube` → `/home/foo/.kube` (dir + kubeconfig
  copy + owner/group); add a task to untaint the control-plane node
  (`kubectl taint nodes host1 node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule-`, idempotent/ignore-errors
  if already removed) so host1's capacity is actually usable — it's the strongest node, not just an etcd
  appliance.
- `ansible/roles/worker/tasks/main.yml`: the "Label node as worker" task references
  `/home/ubuntu/.kube/config`, which was never even consistent with the control-plane role's `rocky` user
  — fix to `/home/foo/.kube/config`.
- The rest of `common`/`containerd`/`kubeadm` roles and `bootstrap.yml`'s structure (common → containerd →
  kubeadm on all nodes, then control-plane init, then worker join) are sound as-is — reuse them, don't
  rewrite.
- **Longhorn storage — resolved by live disk polling**: `group_vars/workers.yml`'s
  `longhorn_data_disk: /dev/sdb` assumed a dedicated Proxmox virtual data disk. Real hardware check
  (`lsblk`) confirms **none of the three hosts have a second disk** — each is single-disk
  (`autopart --type=lvm --nohome`), with several hundred GB of unallocated free space left in the LVM
  volume group (root only took 70GB + swap out of ~475-930GB VGs). Fix: replace `longhorn_data_disk` with
  an `lvcreate` task (new role or extend `common`) that carves an LV (e.g. `lv_longhorn`, sized to leave
  headroom) from each host's free VG space and mounts it at `/var/lib/longhorn` — run on all three hosts
  now that host1 is schedulable too. Skip a dedicated LV on host3 for Longhorn *replica* placement if its
  100 Mb/s NIC link (see README note) isn't fixed first — replication over a 100 Mb link will bottleneck.
- Fetched kubeconfig destination (`clusters/homelab/kubeconfig`, written by the control-plane role's
  `fetch` task) is **not currently gitignored** — add it to `.gitignore` before running this against a
  public repo; the file is a live cluster-admin credential.

## 3. Replace `terraform/proxmox/` with a bootstrap-only module

Delete `terraform/proxmox/` (VM provisioning, `bpg/proxmox` provider — nothing left for it to target) and
add `terraform/cluster-bootstrap/`:

- **Providers**: `hashicorp/kubernetes` and `hashicorp/helm`, both configured via
  `config_path = var.kubeconfig_path` (default `../../clusters/homelab/kubeconfig`, the file Ansible just
  fetched in step 2).
- **`helm_release "argocd"`**: installs the `argo-cd` chart (argoproj Helm repo) into a new `argocd`
  namespace (`create_namespace = true`) — replaces the current plain-manifest
  `clusters/homelab/bootstrap/argocd-install.yml` + the manual `kubectl apply` step documented in
  `docs/argocd-gitops.md`.
- **Root Applications/Projects**: apply the manifests from step 4 below (infra root Application + the
  `prod`/`stage` `AppProject`s and their root Applications) as `kubectl_manifest` resources (use the
  `alekc/kubectl` provider — handles CRDs that don't exist until the ArgoCD Helm release lands, which the
  core `kubernetes_manifest` resource doesn't handle cleanly) with `depends_on = [helm_release.argocd]`.
  Template the `repoURL`/`targetRevision` from variables instead of the current hardcoded `YOUR_USERNAME`
  placeholder.
- **Outputs**: note (in `outputs.tf` or just docs) how to retrieve the ArgoCD-generated admin password:
  `kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d`.
- Local state (`*.tfstate`, already gitignored) is fine here — the same jumpbox runs both the CI runner and
  `terraform apply`, no need for a remote backend for a 3-node homelab.

## 4. Fix the ArgoCD scaffold's stale VM-era values, add prod/stage

`clusters/homelab/` already has the right shape (app-of-apps + per-component Application manifests) for
cluster-wide infra — that part stays a single instance (one Cilium, one MetalLB, etc. — these are
cluster-scoped controllers, not per-environment). Fix the stale values, then add the prod/stage split as a
second, separate concern layered on top for `apps/` (user workloads) only:

**Fix existing infra scaffold:**
- `clusters/homelab/bootstrap/app-of-apps.yml`: `repoURL: https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/k8s-homelab` →
  the real repo URL; this Application keeps pointing at `clusters/homelab/infrastructure` only (rename to
  something like `infra-root` once the prod/stage roots exist alongside it, so the three root Applications
  are distinguishable).
- `clusters/homelab/infrastructure/cilium.yml`: `k8sServiceHost: 192.168.1.101` → `10.10.10.10` (host1,
  the control-plane IP under the corrected topology).
- `clusters/homelab/infrastructure/metallb.yml` (IP pool, currently documented in `docs/networking.md` as
  `192.168.1.200-192.168.1.220`): move into the actual `10.10.10.0/24` range. The Opal's DHCP pool covers
  `10.10.10.2-249` (from `dnsmasq-provisioning.conf`), so use the tail end outside that dynamic range —
  e.g. `10.10.10.250-10.10.10.253` — to avoid a MetalLB VIP colliding with a DHCP-assigned address.
- Sweep the rest of `clusters/homelab/infrastructure/*.yml` (ingress-nginx, cert-manager, longhorn) for any
  other `192.168.1.x` leftovers.

**Add prod/stage separation (namespace-level, single cluster):**
- Two `AppProject`s under `clusters/homelab/bootstrap/` (e.g. `projects.yml`): `prod` restricted to
  destination namespace `prod`, `stage` restricted to destination namespace `stage` — this is what actually
  enforces the isolation (a stage Application can't accidentally deploy into `prod`).
- Restructure `apps/` (currently just empty `apps/argocd/`, `apps/monitoring/` placeholders) into
  `apps/prod/` and `apps/stage/` — each a normal ArgoCD app-of-apps directory (one Application per
  workload you actually add later; no workloads exist yet, so this is just the scaffold).
- Two more root Applications (`apps/prod` and `apps/stage`, project `prod`/`stage` respectively), both
  initially pointed at `targetRevision: main` — same branch, different path, since inventing a
  `develop`-branch promotion workflow isn't needed to get prod/stage isolation working. Note in
  `docs/argocd-gitops.md` that branch-based promotion (`stage` tracking a `develop` branch instead of a
  path on `main`) is a natural upgrade later if a promotion workflow is wanted, not required now.
- `Namespace` manifests for `prod` and `stage` (or `CreateNamespace=true` in each root Application's
  `syncPolicy`).

## 5. CI/CD pipeline

- Register the Mac as a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner with labels `self-hosted, homelab` (needs the
  WireGuard tunnel from step 1 up to reach the hosts/cluster).
- Update `.github/workflows/validate.yml`, `plan.yml`, `deploy.yml`:
  - Swap every `terraform -chdir=terraform/proxmox ...` for `terraform -chdir=terraform/cluster-bootstrap ...`.
  - Drop the now-irrelevant `PROXMOX_*` secrets/env vars from `plan.yml`/`deploy.yml` — the new module
    only needs the kubeconfig Ansible already produced locally on the runner, no remote API credentials.
  - `ansible-playbook` invocations already point at the right paths (`ansible/inventory/hosts.yml`,
    `ansible/playbooks/bootstrap.yml`) — no change needed there beyond what step 2 fixes.
  - `deploy.yml`'s `argocd-verify` job (waits for all ArgoCD Applications to sync/heal) already matches
    this design as-is once the scaffold in step 4 is correct.

## 6. Docs and README cleanup

- Delete `docs/proxmox-setup.md` (no Proxmox host exists to prep).
- Rewrite `docs/terraform.md` for the new `cluster-bootstrap` module's variables (was Proxmox
  endpoint/credentials/node map — now kubeconfig path + repo URL/revision).
- Update `README.md`'s "Getting Started" (currently "Proxmox → Terraform → Ansible → ArgoCD") to: PXE/
  kickstart (done, `bare-metal/`) → WireGuard jumpbox tunnel → Ansible bootstrap → Terraform (ArgoCD
  install) → ArgoCD sync. Update the "Network" section's `192.168.1.0/24` diagram to `10.10.10.0/24`.
- Spot-check `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/ansible.md`, `docs/argocd-gitops.md`, `docs/day2-operations.md`
  for other stale `192.168.1.x` / Proxmox references while touching each for the changes above.

## Verification

1. `ansible -i ansible/inventory/hosts.yml all -m ping` from the jumpbox (over the WG tunnel) — confirms
   inventory + SSH user/key fixes are correct against real hosts.
2. `ansible-playbook -i ansible/inventory/hosts.yml ansible/playbooks/bootstrap.yml` — kubeadm cluster
   comes up, `kubectl get nodes` (using the fetched kubeconfig) shows host1 as control-plane (untainted,
   schedulable), host2/host3 as workers (NotReady is expected until Cilium is installed — no CNI yet).
3. `terraform -chdir=terraform/cluster-bootstrap apply` — ArgoCD pods come up in the `argocd` namespace;
   `kubectl -n argocd get appproject prod stage` and the infra/prod/stage root Applications all exist.
4. Watch ArgoCD sync: `kubectl -n argocd get applications` until all are `Synced`/`Healthy`; `kubectl get
   nodes` should flip to `Ready` once Cilium is running; `cilium status` healthy; `kubectl get ns prod
   stage` exist.
5. `kubectl get svc -A | grep LoadBalancer` gets an IP from the new `10.10.10.250-253` MetalLB pool, not
   stuck `<pending>`.
6. Confirm project isolation: try (as a sanity check, then revert) pointing a `stage`-project Application
   at namespace `prod` and confirm ArgoCD rejects the sync — proves the `AppProject` restriction is real,
   not just a naming convention.
7. Push a trivial change on a branch/PR and confirm the self-hosted runner picks up `validate.yml`/
   `plan.yml` and it passes against the real module path.

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Deploys the provisioning config (dnsmasq + iPXE) onto the GL.iNet Opal.
3	# Run from your MacBook: ./deploy-opal.sh <opal-ip>
4	#
5	# Prerequisites:
6	#   - SSH access to the Opal (root@<opal-ip>), password or key auth already set up
7	#   - Opal's LAN already reconfigured to the isolated provisioning subnet
8	#     (e.g. 10.10.10.1/24) - see router/dnsmasq-provisioning.conf
9	
10	set -euo pipefail
11	
12	OPAL_IP="${1:?Usage: ./deploy-opal.sh <opal-ip>}"
13	SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
14	
15	# dropbear (OpenWrt's SSH server) on this firmware only offers ssh-rsa as a
16	# host key, which recent OpenSSH clients (macOS included) reject by default.
17	SSH_OPTS=(-o HostKeyAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa -o PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms=+ssh-rsa)
18	
19	echo "==> Checking free space on Opal (128MB flash total - keep an eye on this)..."
20	ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" root@"$OPAL_IP" "df -h /overlay"
21	
22	# Confirmed on this firmware: dhcp.@dnsmasq[0].confdir = /tmp/dnsmasq.d,
23	# which is tmpfs (RAM) - anything dropped there is wiped on reboot. So we
24	# keep the real copy in /etc (persistent, survives reboot) and mirror it
25	# into /tmp/dnsmasq.d ourselves, both now and via an /etc/rc.local hook so
26	# it's restored automatically after every power cycle.
27	CONFDIR_PERSIST="/etc/dnsmasq.d"
28	CONFDIR_LIVE="/tmp/dnsmasq.d"
29	
30	echo "==> Installing dnsmasq-full (adds TFTP support) if not already present..."
31	ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" root@"$OPAL_IP" "opkg update && opkg install dnsmasq-full || true"
32	
33	echo "==> Fetching the iPXE boot binary (snponly.efi, ~1MB - UEFI x86_64 targets)..."
34	# snponly.efi (not ipxe.efi) - reuses the UEFI firmware's own NIC driver
35	# (Simple Network Protocol) instead of iPXE's bundled native drivers,
36	# which is the more reliable choice when we don't know if iPXE has a
37	# native driver for this exact NIC (Realtek PCIe GBE here).
38	ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" root@"$OPAL_IP" "mkdir -p /www/ipxe && \
39	  wget -O /www/ipxe/ipxe.efi http://boot.ipxe.org/x86_64-efi/snponly.efi"
40	
41	echo "==> Uploading boot.ipxe (persistent, served by uhttpd from /www)..."
42	ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" root@"$OPAL_IP" "mkdir -p /www && cat > /www/boot.ipxe" < "$SCRIPT_DIR/boot.ipxe"
43	
44	echo "==> Uploading dnsmasq config to a persistent location ($CONFDIR_PERSIST)..."
45	ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" root@"$OPAL_IP" "mkdir -p $CONFDIR_PERSIST && cat > $CONFDIR_PERSIST/provisioning.conf" < "$SCRIPT_DIR/dnsmasq-provisioning.conf"
46	
47	echo "==> Mirroring into $CONFDIR_LIVE and making that survive reboots via rc.local..."
48	ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" root@"$OPAL_IP" "
49	  mkdir -p $CONFDIR_LIVE
50	  cp $CONFDIR_PERSIST/provisioning.conf $CONFDIR_LIVE/provisioning.conf
51	  grep -q provisioning.conf /etc/rc.local || sed -i \"/^exit 0/i mkdir -p $CONFDIR_LIVE; cp $CONFDIR_PERSIST/provisioning.conf $CONFDIR_LIVE/provisioning.conf; /etc/init.d/dnsmasq restart\" /etc/rc.local
52	"
53	
54	echo "==> Restarting dnsmasq..."
55	ssh "${SSH_OPTS[@]}" root@"$OPAL_IP" "/etc/init.d/dnsmasq restart"
56	
57	echo "Done. Enable PXE boot in each mini PC's BIOS/UEFI and power it on -"
58	echo "it should chainload iPXE, then fetch its kickstart from GitHub and"
59	echo "the Rocky mirror directly. No local file staging needed on the Opal."
60
